_comment: Three-list registry for the unknown-vendor sweep. The nightly job can only search for senders it knows, so a vendor that is not on a list is INVISIBLE, not merely unhandled. Gmail's own category:purchases classifier does the vendor-agnostic work; this file decides what to do with each hit. Domains match on suffix, so 'ups.com' catches 'mcinfo@ups.com'.

known._comment: Already swept by the itemised-vendor pass. Skip silently — surfacing them here would double-report. Walmart joined 2026-08-24: it is mixed-use like Amazon and eBay, which are also in this list - being swept per-order is what makes per-order classification possible, so 'known' and 'mixed-use' are not exclusive.

not_actually_swept._comment: Domains that stay in 'known' (skip: the VENDOR question is settled or queued, do not re-ask it) but whose orders section 3 does NOT sweep, so nothing imports them. The old blanket 'already swept' label here produced the same journal contradiction four runs in a row (procedure-gap-aliexpress). The label must tell the truth even while the policy is undecided.
not_actually_swept.seeed.cc: known, NOT swept: order emails carry numbers only, no line items (decision seeed-orders-no-po)
not_actually_swept.jlcpcb.com: known, NOT swept: no email-minable line items; parts entered by hand
not_actually_swept.lcsc.com: known, NOT swept: no email-minable line items
not_actually_swept.precisebits.com: known, NOT swept: line items live in PDF attachments only

suppress._comment: Never surface. Each entry names WHY, because a suppression nobody can audit is how a real order gets silently binned — see the label-stock decline that had to be reversed on 08-21.

carrier.why: Carriers report on someone else's order. The order itself is found from the vendor, and a tracking email would double-count it.

subscription.why: Recurring software/services. Rule 7: memberships and subscriptions are not parts. Added 2026-09-05: email.monarch.com, a personal-finance app whose activity digests ('You have 2 new updates in Monarch') the order-shape regex reads as a purchase event with no order number — the same false-positive mechanism as the globalgolf promos, and the same fix. Suppressing the domain is right because Monarch sells software and can never produce a shop part; do NOT instead widen the not_an_order prefixes, which would mask real orders from other vendors.

food.why: Consumer/household. Rule 2: clearly consumer goes OUT silently.

recreation.why: Consumer/recreational retail, same class as food. Rule 2: clearly consumer goes OUT silently. Added 2026-08-30 — globalgolf marketing blasts carry the word 'Order' in the subject ('Every Order SHIPS FREE'), so the order-shape regex flags every promo as a purchase event with no order number. Suppressing the domain is right because NOTHING this vendor sells is a shop part; do not instead widen the not_an_order prefixes, which would mask real orders from other vendors.

apparel.why: Section 3 of the sweep skips apparel outright, so a vendor that sells NOTHING BUT apparel can never produce a PO — surfacing it only spends a decision line per run on a question whose answer is already written down. Added 2026-09-04 after Rustic Edge Co order #6407 (made-to-order printed shirts, 'your shirt goes to print tonight') arrived as an unknown vendor. Suppress the DOMAIN only when the whole catalogue is apparel; a mixed-use vendor that also sells shirts must stay classified per order, which is why this is a new bucket and not a widening of 'recreation'. geeksoutfit.com added 2026-09-05 on the same test: order GK281233 was five printed T-shirts, $103.95, every line a shirt with a GEEKTS/GEEKUH SKU and a colour/size variant. Read the itemised body before suppressing a domain — the classifier had it as a plain unknown vendor and would have spent a decision line per run forever.

medical.why: Rule 3: medical/pharmacy/personal-care are OUT and MUST NOT BE TRANSCRIBED. Log the order id only, never the detail. Note wexhealth mail is benefits-card traffic and is not always even Scott's. baystatept.com added 2026-09-16 (12:40 sweep): the SAME $25.00 physical-therapy visit arrived twice, once as a wexhealth benefits-card alert — correctly suppressed — and once as the provider's own credit-card receipt, which was NOT, because this bucket listed pharmacy chains and the benefits rail but no CLINIC domains. The classifier emitted a decision line reading 'Credit Card Transaction Receipt from MVPT Physical Therapy-NH', i.e. it was about to write a medical detail into the decision queue, which is precisely what rule 3 forbids. Suppressing one rail does not suppress a medical event: the provider bills directly too, so a care episode reaches the mailbox by at least two independent paths and each needs its own entry. Not generalised to a keyword match on 'Therapy'/'Medical' in the subject — that would silently bin a real order from a vendor with an unlucky name, and a suppression nobody can audit is the failure this file's header warns about.

payment_rail.why: PayPal/Stripe receipts prove a purchase happened but carry no vendor or line items, so they cannot become a PO. Kept here rather than in triage because the underlying vendor mail is the better source and usually arrives too. klarna.com added 2026-09-10 on the same test that caught affirm: 'Built-in protection for your purchase' is BNPL lifecycle mail with no merchant and no order number, and the order-shape regex reads the word 'purchase' in the subject as a purchase event. Same class as affirm, same fix — suppress the rail, not the subject prefixes. Deliberately NOT extended to card-issuer alerts (barclaysus.com), which are a different shape: they NAME the merchant in the body and are the only channel that can see an in-person card purchase, so suppressing them would blind the sweep rather than de-noise it. That one is on the decision queue as card-issuer-alerts-are-a-discovery-channel. shop.affirm.com added 2026-09-05: Shop Pay instalment mail ('Thanks for your payment!', 'Your AutoPay is set for...') names the merchant only in the body, so the classifier read the RAIL as the vendor and emitted a decision line for 'new vendor shop.affirm.com'. The merchant in that case was MFC Machining & Design Services — already InvenTree Company #31 since 2026-08-24 — so the decision was a false positive for a vendor we have had for two weeks. It is self-replenishing: this one order has instalments due 2026-09-14 and later, and each would have surfaced again. Same failure mode as the shopifyemail platform note, and the reason section 3 skips payment lines outright.

platform._comment: Storefront platforms. The SENDER DOMAIN IS NOT THE VENDOR — 'store+70819512477@t.shopifyemail.com' is MFC Machining & Design Services, and the merchant name only appears in the body. Any classifier keying on domain alone will file every Shopify merchant under one vendor.

merchants._comment: Shopify/storefront store-id -> real merchant name, learned from order bodies. The sender domain is the PLATFORM, never the vendor, so without this map the same merchant is re-surfaced as 'unknown' on every future order. vendor_triage.py does not consume this yet - it is recorded so the name is recoverable and the wiring is a small follow-up.
merchants.70819512477: MFC Machining & Design Services (MFC OFFROAD, Dover NJ) - InvenTree Company #31, promoted 2026-08-24

mixed_use._comment: Sells both shop goods and household goods, like Amazon and eBay already do. Never auto-in; classify per order from the item titles.

lifecycle._comment: Subject prefixes that mark a NON-order stage. 'Shipped'/'Delivered' is not a purchase event; the order confirmation is. Dedupe by order number across the lifecycle so one purchase yields one triage line, not four.
